title: Man's Search for Meaning
author: Viktor E. Frankl
theme: Even when almost everything is taken away, a person can still choose how to respond, and a clear reason to live gives the strength to endure.
summary: Viktor Frankl was a Vienna psychiatrist who spent about three years in Nazi concentration camps, including Auschwitz, and lost his parents, his brother and his wife to them. Soon after his release he wrote this short book around one hard question: what keeps a person going when nearly everything has been taken away?

The first part describes camp life as a doctor watching himself and others. Prisoners passed through stages: shock on arrival, then a dull apathy that shielded them from constant pain, and after liberation a strange numbness and sometimes bitterness. Frankl noticed that those with something waiting for them, a child at home, a book to finish, a person to see again, held up far better than those who had given up on the future. When hope went, the body often followed.

He also saw men share their last bread and comfort others. Marching to work in the cold, he held his wife's image in his mind and felt that love reaches far beyond a person's physical presence. From all this he concluded that even when outer freedom is gone, one freedom remains: the freedom to choose our attitude.

The second part introduces logotherapy, his approach to therapy. Its central claim is that our deepest drive is neither pleasure nor power but the search for meaning. Meaning can be found in three ways: through work or a deed we give to the world, through experiencing goodness, beauty or love for another person, and through the courage we bring to suffering we cannot avoid.

For families the message is practical. Meaning is not invented in our heads but found in our duties to the people and tasks in front of us. Asking what life is asking of me today, rather than what I am getting from life, can turn ordinary duties into a quiet source of strength.
takeaway: This week, when a day feels heavy, pause and ask what this moment is asking of you, and name one person or task that gives you a reason to carry on.

questions.q: What was Viktor Frankl's profession before and after his time in the camps?
questions.why: Frankl was a psychiatrist and neurologist in Vienna, which is why he observed camp life with a doctor's eye.

questions.q: What name did Frankl give to his approach to therapy?
questions.why: Logotherapy comes from the Greek 'logos', meaning, and centres on helping people find meaning in life.

questions.q: According to Frankl, what is the deepest human drive?
questions.why: He set the will to meaning against Freud's emphasis on pleasure and Adler's emphasis on power.

questions.q: Which freedom did Frankl say no one can take away?
questions.why: Even when outer freedoms are removed, a person can still decide how to respond inwardly to circumstances.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of Frankl's three ways of finding meaning?
options: Creating a work or doing a deed
questions.why: His three paths are work or deeds, love and experience, and attitude toward suffering; wealth and status are not among them.

questions.q: Which prisoners did Frankl observe tended to endure the camps better?
options: Those who had someone or something waiting for them in the future
Those who kept away from all other prisoners
Those who had been wealthy before
questions.why: A future goal, a loved one or an unfinished task gave a reason to live that sustained people through hardship.

questions.q: What did thinking of his wife during the camp marches teach Frankl about love?
options: That love fades quickly under hardship
That love is mainly a physical feeling
That love only matters in times of comfort
That love reaches beyond a person's physical presence
questions.why: He felt deeply connected to her in his mind, without knowing whether she was alive, and saw that love goes beyond the body.

questions.q: What did Frankl mean by the 'existential vacuum'?
options: A sense of inner emptiness and lack of purpose
The silence of the camps at night
A shortage of food and rest
A gap between two schools of psychology
questions.why: He used the term for the feeling of meaninglessness he saw spreading in modern life.

questions.q: Which shift in question did Frankl recommend?
options: From 'Who is to blame?' to 'How can I escape?'
From 'What do others think?' to 'What do I want?'
From 'What do I expect from life?' to 'What does life expect from me?'
From 'Why me?' to 'Why not someone else?'
questions.why: Turning the question around makes us responsible for answering life through our actions and choices.

options: All suffering should be sought out because it builds character
Suffering that cannot be avoided can still carry meaning through the attitude we take
questions.why: He held that avoidable suffering should be removed, but unavoidable suffering can be met with courage and dignity.
